Properties —

Advanced settings are optional. The main workflow is one image, one preset, Generate, inspect, export.

Rolls the wrap seam into the middle of the image and feathers it there, so the borders become true neighbours — the classic offset-blend method, done for you.

Estimates the broad lighting in linear light with an edge-aware filter, so shadow bleeding across material edges (the usual delight halo) does not happen. Leave it off when the photo is already evenly lit.

Experimental estimators

Optional alternatives for manual review. The existing automatic estimator and material presets remain the normal workflow.

Choose the visible top layer. Only an explicit bare-conductor choice enables metallic; coating and rust remain dielectric. This is an authored identity hint.

The material or coating supplies an uncalibrated starting prior. Enter 0–1 to author a different baseline; this is not a measured GGX roughness fit.

20 mm
35%

AO uses accepted physical height only and stays white for relative height. Strength is intentionally conservative; review it against the final renderer.

Photoreal v1 keeps unmarked maps neutral. V2 can suggest uncalibrated relative relief from repeated low-chroma masonry, wood, or ceramic seams; inspect the result. Finish and metal remain artist-guided.

0%

Used only by the photoreal route for Photograph intent. Starts at 0 because one image cannot reliably separate illumination from pigment. Inspect the base-color and relit previews before increasing it.

Physical scale

Physical mode uses a conservative fixed conversion from the estimated signal, then maps values through this artist-authored range and the X/Y dimensions. The photo does not measure depth; the actual height field may use less than the full range. Height contrast, normal strength, cleanup, and micro-normal controls apply only in Artistic mode.

Structure-gated multiband log-luminance, read from the un-delighted photo so the stitch and weave shading survives. Detail intensity lifts the stitch, weave or crack scale under an edge-aware filter until it reads as a real surface; Detail size chooses which element size that is (1× = the detected one, shown above); Scratch depth carves thin dark features in, Micro detail brings thin bright ones out. Sensor grain stays gated out.

Scharr gradient of the height map with a resolution-independent slope, so the same photo keeps the same apparent bump size at 1K, 2K and 4K. Only the export copy is flipped for DirectX.

How far the height map drives the preview surface, which is what makes the parallax look. A viewing control: the exported maps are unchanged.

The base colour grade — Sampler's HSL / recolour pass, applied to the albedo after the preset has done its repair, so your edit always wins. Hue, saturation and brightness work on the colour map alone; the tint pulls the colour toward that swatch while every bit of fold and grain detail stays in place. Height, normals, roughness and AO never change here. Neutral settings are a true no-op, so an untouched project exports exactly as before.

Driven by photo luminance mixed with local micro-relief energy: where the surface has more fine geometry it scatters light, so it reads rougher. That keeps the map physical instead of "shadows = gloss".

Reflectance strength of non-metals: 1 = the physical 4%. Take it to 0 and a fully rough surface stops reflecting entirely; raise it for wet or lacquered coatings. Metals ignore it, their reflection colour is their own albedo.

Auto reads metal from the photo: thin, crisp highlights over bright, colour-neutral areas. Most photos are not metal — always check the map by eye, and use Manual for a known metal surface.

Source checks run on every build: how much evidence this photo actually carries per channel.

Apply the detail image to specific material maps. Base takes its colour; Height and Roughness take its tone; Metallic and AO are lowered by its dark areas. Every channel you tick gets its own Strength and Blend under its chips. Nothing is applied until you tick a channel.

The detail image is applied at Amount - scaled again by each channel's own Strength - and tiled at the Tiling scale.

Generated patterns (noise, grunge, grain) that push into the maps you tick. They are not layers and never change the photo.

Horizon-based occlusion computed on the height field: every pixel measures the tallest occluding horizon in 8 directions, then the map is joint-upsampled along the height edges. Real contact shading in creases, not a blurred height map.

Transparency is how much light passes through the surface: 0 is solid, 1 is clear glass. Presets set it for you (glass and water 0.95, wax and honey lower, most materials 0). Transparency roughness frosts it: 0 is a clean window, higher scatters whatever is behind the surface.

Surface ripple puts gently moving waves on the preview surface — it is what makes water read as water. It is a preview effect: the exported normal map still carries the photo's own relief. Set it to 0 to keep the photo relief instead.

Pick a map, then drag the three sliders: the histogram is that map's tone distribution (sampled before any clipping, so it stays put while you drag), the gold lines are where Black/White cut, and the map card and 3D preview follow live. 0 / 1 / 1 is untouched.

Black point, white point and gamma per finished map — a non-destructive remap that puts each channel in the range an engine expects (lift the height’s black point, tighten roughness’s spread). 0 / 1 / 1 is identity, and every map keeps its own values. The 16-bit height export follows the height’s curve too; maps derived from the height field itself (normal, AO) stay as computed.

Paint = keep the computed map inside the stroke. Outside falls back to a neutral PER MAP (metal → 0, height → flat, roughness → the material’s base roughness, AO / opacity → untouched), so masking metal never flattens the other channels. Tick only the maps this mask is for.

Paint where the effect applies: covered areas keep the computed map, everything else becomes the outside value (0 = effect only where painted, e.g. metal along the mortar line only). Pick the underlay above to paint against any map; brush size is in screen pixels.

Pick a look to stylise the source image before the material is derived. Base colour, height, normals and roughness all follow the same stylised image, so the material stays consistent.

Heavy looks (oil, watercolor, anime) take a few seconds at 2K — set Preview resolution to 1K while you tune, then raise the Output resolution for the final export.

Studio lighting — 3D view. Sun angle, height, size and intensity, rig and environment shape every preview, raster and ray-traced. The sun is drawn in the sky where it really is, so moving the angle moves the shadow with it, and the compass in the viewport corner shows where the light is coming from. The checkboxes at the bottom are viewport helpers.

Background — standard view only. What sits behind the object in the normal 3D preview. It is not a light source, and the ray-traced view (R) ignores it: that view renders the environment instead.

Environment — lighting and reflections. The built-in studio sky, or an HDR / EXR loaded with the HDRI button in the viewer bar. It lights the material, shows up in reflections, and is the sky the ray-traced view (R) renders. Environment intensity and rotation above shape it, and the Lighting environment preset below picks the sky itself (it replaces a loaded HDRI).

Ray exposure and ray bounces affect the ray-traced view (R) only. Ray bounces is how far light travels: 2-3 is flat but fast, 4 is the default, 5-6 adds depth and costs time per sample.

Image2PBR — workflow and limits

Created by Jeremy Zhang · Image2PBR v6.1.0 · offline, single-file build

Image2PBR is a local, browser-based image-to-PBR material workspace — a deterministic, inspectable counterpart to Substance 3D Sampler's B2M path. The image never leaves this machine; it writes a standard material map bundle for a DCC tool or game engine.

Single file, no network. The material engine, the art-style engine, the path tracer and every library (three.js, JSZip, pako) are inlined in this page: it makes zero external requests and works offline.

Workflow

  • Import a photo (PNG / JPG / WEBP / TGA) or drag it anywhere on the window. Flat, front-facing, evenly lit surfaces work best.
  • Look (optional) — pick an art style in Art style. The stylised image becomes the single source for every map, so base colour, height, normals, roughness and AO stay consistent.
  • Shape the material: Seamless tiling, Lighting removal, Height, Normal, Roughness, Metallic, Ambient occlusion. Every control has a tooltip, double-click resets one control, ↺ resets a whole section, and Ctrl+Z undoes parameter changes. Two controls worth knowing: Shading removed (how much of the photo's lighting is divided out — less keeps more of the original contrast in the base colour) and Noise cleanup (cleans 1-pixel slope noise out of the height before the normal map is derived). The time in the header is how long the last full generation took.
  • Validate, then click any map card to inspect that channel on the 3D preview. The report measures every map against the one thing that matters when a texture repeats: the step across the tile seam divided by the steps right beside it. 1.0 means the seam is invisible; above ~1.5 it will show when the material is tiled. It also reports height floor/ceiling clipping, roughness spread, the metallic average and the source size.
  • Export — pick an engine preset and the output resolution, then download single maps or the whole bundle (every map + packed texture + material.json + README).

Layers: combining images into one texture

A texture is rarely one photo. The Layers panel under the source image stacks several — brick with plaster patches, tiles with a grout overlay, dirt on top of a clean surface — and combines them into one new image. That combined image is what the pipeline reads, so the every map, the presets, the art styles, the ray-traced view and every export follow the stack automatically.

  • The bottom layer is the base — it sets the size and aspect of the result. Every layer above it is placed into that frame.
  • Weight is how strongly a layer mixes over everything below it: 100 % replaces, 50 % is an even mix, 0 % is invisible but keeps its settings. The eye hides a layer completely, ✕ deletes it, and rows drag up and down (or focus one and press ↑/↓).
  • Blend mode picks the maths: Normal, Multiply, Screen, Overlay, Soft light, Hard light, Add, Subtract, Difference, Exclusion, Darken, Lighten. Blending is done in linear light with the same formulas Substance uses, so a 50 % mix here looks like a 50 % mix there.
  • Combine → Weighted changes the model to a normalised average: each layer's weight is its share of the whole, so 50 / 30 / 20 adds up to 100 % exactly. Blend modes do not apply in that mode — the weights are the whole story. Stacked (the default) is the Photoshop-style “each layer over the ones below”.
  • Scale of 1 fills the frame; below 1 the image tiles, which is how you lay a small pattern over a big surface. Rotation turns the layer (tiles turn with it) and Offset slides it — the pattern keeps repeating past the edge, so a seamless texture stays seamless.
  • Brightness / Contrast / Invert match a layer to the others before they are mixed: two photos are almost never exposed the same way, and these are applied in sRGB exactly like a Photoshop adjustment.
  • Up to 8 layers. Fit whole image shrinks the selected layer until it all fits, Reset layer puts it back to weight 100 % filling the frame, Duplicate copies it.

Staying smooth. While you drag a layer control the app recomposites and re-derives the maps at a small size and pushes that straight to the viewport, so the blend reacts under your hand; when you let go it rebuilds at full working resolution. The exported material always comes from the full-resolution composite, and the layer recipe is written into the bundle's material.json so a material can be audited or rebuilt later.

The 3D viewport

  • Raster preview (default) — real-time PBR with the studio rig, a lit floor, a two-tier ground grid and a soft shadow that anchors the object.
  • Ray button (or R) switches to a progressive path-traced preview: real global illumination, area-light soft shadows, environment importance sampling, three bounces and an AgX filmic view transform. It keeps refining while the camera and material stay still, resets on any change, and converges at 6000 samples.
  • Lighting rig — Studio 3-point (key · fill · rim), Studio 6-point (adds top · bounce · back), Single key + ambient, or HDR environment only. Key light angle rotates the rig, Key intensity scales it.
  • Grid button (or G) toggles the ground grid; Ground shadow catcher toggles the lit studio floor under the object.
  • HDRI loads an HDR / EXR studio environment (or drop it on the viewport). The environment drives reflections in both modes; Environment rotation rebuilds it.
  • The ray-traced preview needs WebGL2 with float render targets and is deterministic — the same camera, material and seed always give the same image.

Art styles (looks)

  • Cartoon · cel shaded — edge-preserving Kuwahara flattening, luminance posterisation and ink outlines: a painted toon texture for stylised games.
  • Anime background · painted — strong structure-preserving flattening, soft tonal steps and thin soft lines: hand-painted background feel.
  • Pixel art — area downsample onto a real pixel grid, median-cut palette, optional ordered dithering, upscaled back to working resolution.
  • Watercolor — flattening, soft washes, wet-edge darkening and paper grain with granulation.
  • Oil painting — sector Kuwahara brushwork aligned to the measured flow direction, plus a subtle canvas weave.
  • Ink · cross-hatch — tonal cross-hatching on a warm paper tone with outlines.

Quick looks (Toon, Anime BG, Pixel 96, Watercolor, Oil, Ink) set a full starting point — the four sliders below them are relabelled by the selected look. Style amount blends the stylised result back toward the untouched photo.

Engine presets

  • Generic PBR — separate maps, engine-agnostic names.
  • Unreal Engine 5 — T_Name_BC / _N / _ORM / _H, DirectX normal, ORM packed as R = AO, G = Roughness, B = Metallic.
  • Unity HDRP — MaskMap packed as R = Metallic, G = AO, B = Detail, A = Roughness, OpenGL normal.
  • glTF 2.0 / three.js — baseColor / normal / metallicRoughness / occlusion packing.

What makes this build physically better

  • Height — a structure tensor measures the local flow direction first; detail is averaged along it and micro detail below its own robust noise floor is removed, so sensor grain never becomes fake relief.
  • Delight — the illumination estimate is edge-aware (guided filter in linear light). That is exactly where naive delighters produce halos across material edges.
  • Normals — Scharr gradients of the height field with a resolution-independent slope: the same photo keeps the same apparent bump size at 1K–4K.
  • Roughness — photo luminance mixed with local micro-relief energy, so glossy/matte follows surface structure instead of "shadows = gloss". While a material preset is active its class range owns this channel; as soon as you move Roughness or Metallic yourself, your values are what ship (pick the preset again, or Reset, to hand the channel back).
  • AO — horizon-based occlusion on the height field (8 directions, tallest horizon wins), joint-upsampled along height edges: real contact shading, not a blurred height.
  • Seamless — the offset-blend method: the wrap seam is rolled into the middle and feathered there, so the borders become true neighbours and the tile repeats cleanly. On by default because the tool makes tiling materials; turn it off for decals or trim sheets where the original framing matters more than the repeat.

Resolution, colour and conventions

  • Work at 2K: 1K is instant, 3–4K takes several seconds per rebuild. Set Output resolution to 4K for the final export.
  • Heavy looks (oil, watercolor, anime) add a few seconds at 2K — drop the preview to 1K while tuning.
  • Base color is sRGB. Normal, Height, Roughness, Metallic, AO and Opacity are linear data — never assign a colour profile to them. Height ships as 16-bit PNG (big-endian) plus an 8-bit fallback. Packed engine textures are always lossless PNG; the viewer always shows the OpenGL orientation while the exported normal follows the convention you pick.

Honest limits

  • This is a deterministic B2M-grade estimator. Lighting, geometry and material are entangled in a single image, so no single photo uniquely determines albedo, height, normals, roughness and metalness. It is not a trained neural network and not a calibrated scan.
  • Metallic auto is a neutral-brightness mask, not a material classifier.
  • For hero assets, compare the result against a scan or a multi-light capture at final texel density before delivery.

What images work best

Every map is derived from this one image, so the photo sets the ceiling on quality. The estimator reads a flat surface of a single material; it cannot invent detail that is not in the pixels.

  • Flat and front-facing. Shoot square to the surface - a tilted shot or a wide-angle lens bakes perspective into the height and the normals.
  • Even, soft light. Diffuse light with no hard shadow and no hot specular highlight. The lighting-removal stage flattens a gentle gradient well; it cannot undo a cast shadow or a blown-out highlight.
  • One material, filling the frame. No other objects, no material edges, no fingers, no photographer's shadow.
  • Sharp and clean. In focus, no motion blur, no heavy JPEG mush. Sharpness becomes the finest detail in the height and normal maps; blur becomes a soft, waxy surface.
  • Enough resolution. 2K or more on the long edge if you want fine grain - the maps are generated at the preview / output resolution you choose, not beyond the source.
  • Neutral colour. A colour cast makes every material look the same colour. If the source is strongly tinted, pick a preset whose tint matches the real material and it will be re-hued toward the measured chromaticity.
  • Tileable sources tile best. If the photo's left and right edges do not match, "Seamless tiling" can only hide the seam; a source that wraps or repeats is perfect.
  • Good sources: material libraries, scanned swatches, controlled studio shots, flat lay-downs, top-down scans. Weak sources: phone snaps in mixed light, screenshots of other renders, anything with painted-in lighting, watermarks or text.

If the material comes out flat or wrong, fix the source before the settings: crop tighter to the material, straighten the perspective, and even out the light.

One material, every view and every engine

The raster view, the ray-traced view and the exported maps all describe the same material: metalness 1 × the metallic map, roughness 1 × the roughness map, the same UVs and tiling, the same AO, and the same ACES tone curve (the ray tracer ports three.js's exact curve). The tracer also receives the same environment strength and the same hemisphere fill as the raster material, and it is lit by a rig calibrated against the raster's lights (measured 2.27×, they are different light models).

What still differs, honestly: a path tracer integrates real light transport — multiple bounces, soft shadows, real refraction — so a very bright diffuse material reads ~1.5× dimmer than the raster view, which clips its highlights and adds its own fill. Metals, the case people notice first, now match closely (measured within ~10% in level, and within ±0.01 in hue).

Taking it into Blender, UE5 or Unity: the maps are the contract, and the manifest records the facts a downstream renderer needs (metallic-roughness workflow, roughness/metallic factors of 1, the normal convention, and Unity's MaskMap alpha as smoothness = 1 − roughness). Match these three things and the material lands where you expect it:

  • Blender — Principled BSDF: BaseColor (sRGB) → Base Color, Roughness/Metallic (linear) → the respective inputs, Normal (either convention) → Normal Map, IOR from the manifest for glass, water, honey. Set the view transform to Standard or Filmic; Blender 4.x defaults to AgX, which will look flatter than this preview no matter what the maps say.
  • Unreal Engine 5 — use the Unreal preset (T_ prefix, DirectX normals, packed ORM: R = AO, G = Roughness, B = Metallic), drop ORM into the Mask input of a Material with Metallic/Roughness/Occlusion sampling R/G/B.
  • Unity HDRP — use the Unity preset: the MaskMap is R = Metallic, G = AO, B = Detail (0.5), A = Smoothness (1 − roughness), exactly as HDRP expects.
  • glTF / three.js — baseColor in sRGB, metallicRoughness in linear (G = Roughness, B = Metallic), AO separate.

Lighting is never part of a texture set, so the preview cannot dictate an engine's lights — but the material itself now behaves the same everywhere it is put.

Credits

  • Image2PBR — created by Jeremy Zhang. Version 6.0 · layer stack, live compositing, ray-traced cloth.
  • Fabric preview mesh: fabric1.glb, modelled by Jeremy Zhang in Blender — meshopt-decoded, recentred to the 2.7-unit preview convention and repacked at build time.
  • One self-contained offline file: three.js r145, JSZip, pako, and the in-house material, art-style and path-tracing engines. No network requests, ever.

The fabric model is real geometry in both views. The ray-traced view builds a bounding-volume hierarchy over the cloth's 12,174 triangles and traces them directly, so the base, normal, roughness, metallic and AO maps shade it exactly as they shade the sphere or cube — folds, hem and weave detail included. Its hem rests just above the floor plane, and the tracer's floor sits at the same height as the one in the standard view, so the two views agree on where the model stands.

Shortcuts and UI

  • Space regenerate · 1–5 preview model · M cycle channels · R ray-traced preview · G ground grid · Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z undo / redo · Esc close this dialog
  • Drag the dividers to resize panels; collapse the map shelf from its handle. The Properties tabs (All / Surface / Style / Preview) filter the sections.
  • Every slider has exactly one editable value box with its unit — type a number instead of dragging.
